title: ML System Design Interview Framework
interviewAnswer: Start with product requirements and constraints, then define data, labels, metrics, baseline, training pipeline, serving path, storage, scale, monitoring, failure modes and iteration loop. Architecture should follow requirements—not precede them.
why: System-design interviews reward structured trade-off thinking. A brilliant model choice cannot rescue an architecture that ignores requirements or data reality.
intuition: Start by asking what users need and what failure costs. Then work backward from the serving requirement into data, model, training and operational components.
deepDive: A reliable sequence is: clarify functional/non-functional requirements → define success metrics → understand data/labels → baseline/model → training pipeline → serving path → storage/interfaces → scale/cost → monitoring/retraining → privacy/security → failure modes. Explicitly separate online and offline paths.
math: Useful back-of-envelope math: QPS × payload size → bandwidth; model latency × concurrency → compute; data/day → storage; batch size ↔ throughput/latency.
code:
# Interview whiteboard checklist
requirements()
data_and_labels()
offline_metrics()
training_pipeline()
serving_path()
scale_and_cost()
monitoring_and_feedback()
failures_and_security()
commonMistakes: Jumping directly to “use Kafka/Kubernetes/SageMaker” before requirements.
Ignoring label availability and feedback loops.
No operational metric or failure plan.
followUps: How would this change at 100× traffic?
What if labels arrive a month later?
How do you prevent training-serving skew?
What is the cheapest simpler version?
production: Prefer the simplest architecture that meets SLOs. Every added queue, feature store or cluster creates operational cost and new failure modes.
workedExample: For a heavy reconstruction model, requirements may immediately imply async jobs, object storage and GPU workers instead of a synchronous REST prediction.
